name: mixteco de Magdalena Peñasco
catalog_citation: Hollenbach, Elena Erickson de. 2004 [mayo 2004; (c) 2004 Instituto Lingüístico de Verano, A.C.]. Los tonos del mixteco de Magdalena Peñasco. SIL-Mexico (47 pp; downloaded via the Internet Archive id_ capture of www.sil.org/mexico/mixteca/magdale…
catalog_quote: Las palabras del mixteco tienen un núcleo de dos sílabas con el acento prosódico en la primera. Este grupo bisílabo es de mucha importancia en la fonología de la lengua, y se presentan los tonos de este grupo antes de considerar las palabras más largas o más cortas. ... El tono bajo, cuando recibe el acento prosódico, que cae en la primera sílaba del grupo bisílabo, se actualiza como un desliz del tono medio al tono bajo. ... la palabra compuesta de tres sílabas nd¢k¢tª ‘lavar’ tiene el acento prosódico en la sílaba k¢ ... Las palabras nativas de tres sílabas son todas formas compuestas. La mayoría se compone de un prefijo más una raíz de dos sílabas. ... Los préstamos del español han entrado al mixteco con varios patrones tonales, según el acento prosódico de la palabra en español. En su forma mixteca, la gran mayoría de estas palabras tiene el acento prosódico en la penúltima sílaba, …

new_statements.quote: Las palabras del mixteco tienen un núcleo de dos sílabas con el acento prosódico en la primera. [p.1] ... El tono bajo, cuando recibe el acento prosódico, que cae en la primera sílaba del grupo bisílabo, se actualiza como un desliz del tono medio al tono bajo. [p.2] ... la palabra compuesta de tres sílabas nd¢k¢tª ‘lavar’ tiene el acento prosódico en la sílaba k¢ [p.6] ... En su forma mixteca, la gran mayoría de estas palabras tiene el acento prosódico en la penúltima sílaba, de acuerdo con los patrones para palabras nativas. [p.33] ... Hay un grupo de palabras funcionales (partículas) que no reciben un acento prosódico, y tienen una sola vocal. [p.35]
new_statements.translation: Mixtec words have a nucleus of two syllables with the prosodic stress on the first. [p.1] ... Low tone, when it receives the prosodic stress, which falls on the first syllable of the bisyllabic group, is realized as a glide from mid tone to low tone. [p.2] ... the three-syllable compound word nd¢k¢tª 'to wash' has the prosodic stress on the syllable k¢ [p.6] ... In their Mixtec form, the great majority of these words [Spanish loans] have the prosodic stress on the penultimate syllable, in accordance with the patterns for native words. [p.33] ... There is a group of function words (particles) that do not receive a prosodic stress and have a single vowel. [p.35]

new_statements.relation_note: This is the very source the catalog record (penultimate stress, penult) was built from; all five quoted sentences were re-read in the text we hold layer at the stated pages and match the catalog quote verbatim. The catalog's date '2005' (from the Glottolog listing) differs from the PDF's own '[mayo 2004]'; the the full catalog already carries the corrected 2004 date and 47 pp. The only caveat is that the '0010' cell for four-syllable words rests on the loan 'presidente' and the author's penult equation, not on an explicit statement about native four-syllable compounds.
new_statements.rule_in_words: There is no separate stress section; stress (acento prosódico) is stated inside the tone description. Every native word is built on a bisyllabic root couplet stressed on its first syllable; native trisyllables are prefix + couplet, so stress sits on the root-initial syllable (nd¢-k¢-tª stressed on k¢), which is the penult of the word. Spanish loans of 2-4 syllables (libro, Castilla, barato, presidente) overwhelmingly take penultimate stress, which the author explicitly equates with the native pattern. Monosyllabic particles (proclitics, enclitics) carry no stress and are written as separate words. Native 4- and 5-syllable compounds (sec. 3.1 pp.32-33) are listed with tone patterns only; their stress position is not stated, so word lengths above three rest on the loan example plus the author's penult equation. Stress coexists with three-level lexical tone and conditions its realization (stressed low = mid-to-low glide; unstressed mid syllables are the targets of low-tone spreading). No weight conditioning is mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: fn.6 p.7 (hedged): 'Es muy probable que el tono alto en la última sílaba haya atraído el acento prosódico a ésta, y la sílaba penúltima se percibe como otra sílaba átona que se deja cambiar al tono bajo' (final high tone in m.a(b) words may attract stress to the final syllable). Sec. 2.1 p.7: 'A veces un verbo copulativo se pronuncia sin acento prosódico y las dos sílabas se cambian al tono bajo.' fn.14 p.33: 'Las personas menores de edad y más bilingües en español pronuncian estas palabras [préstamos esdrújulos] con el acento prosódico en la sílaba antepenúltima, como en español'. Sec. 3.3 p.35: monosyllabic particles are unstressed.
new_statements.identity_note: Work 1 describes the Mixtec of the municipio of Magdalena Peñasco, distrito de Tlaxiaco, Oaxaca (fn.1 p.1); fn.13 (p.29) notes that the neighbouring San Cristóbal Amoltepec variety, and some speakers in northern Magdalena, lack one prefix-root tone restriction. The site bibliography notes that the same glottocode also groups Santo Domingo Huendio (Becerra Roldán 2015, not yet obtained), for which no stress statement has been checked. Work 0's author Barbara E. Hollenbach is the same person as Elena Erickson de Hollenbach.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim in the held 2004 SIL tone paper at all stated locators. The classification (stress on the first syllable of the bisyllabic root = penult of the orthographic word; loans mostly penult) rests on a first-hand phonology article by the language's describer, and the best available source, her 2013 475-pp reference grammar, is already held by the project and independently states the same rule in sec. 2.5 pp.22-23 (stress always on root-initial syllable; penult in words ending in a plain vowel; first mora of a final long/glottalized vowel; clitics unstressed and written separately; 'el acento es muy regular'). Nothing in either source suggests a different coding; the only nuances (CVV-final roots stressed on the first part of the vowel; weak stress sometimes heard on a H-toned final syllable; bilingual speakers' Spanish-pattern loans) are already compatible with the record's the primary-stress rule/ex
